lesson.title: Chasing Perfect Area: What Happens as the Rectangles Vanish
lesson.summary: A Riemann sum only ever approximates the area under a curve, but watching what happens as the rectangles get infinitely thin and infinitely numerous reveals a single exact number hiding inside the approximation.
lesson.body:
A Riemann sum is built from a compromise. You slice the interval from a to b into n pieces, put a rectangle on each piece using the function's height at some sample point, and add up the areas. No matter how carefully you choose those sample points, the rectangles either poke above the curve or leave gaps below it, so the sum is always a little bit wrong. The natural question is whether that error can be controlled, and it can: as you use more rectangles, each one gets thinner, so the sliver of error trapped inside any single rectangle shrinks along with it.

This is the idea behind the limit of a Riemann sum. Instead of stopping at some fixed number of rectangles, imagine letting n grow without bound, so the width of each rectangle, usually written as delta x, shrinks toward 0. What is remarkable, and what took mathematicians real work to prove, is that the sum settles down. It does not wander or oscillate forever. It approaches one specific real number, and it approaches that same number whether you sampled with left endpoints, right endpoints, or midpoints, as long as the function is reasonably well behaved, such as continuous on the interval. That settling down is what makes area under a curve a legitimate, well defined mathematical object instead of just a rough estimate that depends on how you happened to draw the rectangles.

Here is a fully worked example. Let f(x) = x^2 on the interval [0, 1], and build a right endpoint Riemann sum with n equal subintervals. Each subinterval has width delta x = 1/n, and the right endpoint of the i-th subinterval is x_i = i/n. The sum is R_n = sum from i = 1 to n of f(x_i) times delta x = sum of (i/n)^2 times (1/n) = (1/n^3) times the sum of i^2 from 1 to n. Using the standard formula sum of i^2 from 1 to n = n(n+1)(2n+1)/6, this becomes R_n = n(n+1)(2n+1) / (6n^3), which simplifies to (n+1)(2n+1) / (6n^2). Expanding the numerator gives 2n^2 + 3n + 1, so R_n = 1/3 + 1/(2n) + 1/(6n^2). As n grows toward infinity, the terms 1/(2n) and 1/(6n^2) both shrink to 0, so R_n approaches exactly 1/3. No matter how large you make n, the leftover terms keep shrinking, and the limit locks onto 1/3.

This example ties together the two ideas this chapter builds on. From the concept of a Riemann sum, you get the raw sum R_n and its geometric meaning as approximate area. From the concept of a limit, you get the precise language for saying what happens as n grows without bound, rather than just eyeballing that the numbers seem to be settling near 1/3. Put those two ideas together and you get a single exact number attached to the region under f(x) = x^2 from 0 to 1. That number, produced by this exact limiting process for any reasonably well behaved function on any interval, is what the next chapter names the definite integral.
